The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, necessitates the analysis of its planets' potential resonant behavior. By using existing parameters in N-body simulations, our analysis confirms that nearly all simulations (99.2%) produce a chain of 3:2 resonances; however, fewer (11%) demonstrate a five-planet resonance chain. We successfully employ resonances to confine the orbital periods and masses of the planets. In contrast to an in situ formation, our results suggest that super-Earths K2-138 b, c, e, and f, and planet d (with a high probability of being a super-Earth) could have primarily composed of rock, whereas the more massive planets d, e, and f might contain a substantial water content. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on solving small-scale optimization subproblems, but this proves computationally expensive and hinders the application to even smaller subsets of constraints. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an end-to-end machine learning approach, where data-driven models derived from supervised learning predict whether a constraint is valid or not, thereby accelerating the solution process. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach can achieve a significant reduction in computation time, namely an average decrease of 68.6% compared to state-of-the-art constraint screening methods, while also increasing the number of constraints that can be safely ignored, namely up to 94.1% of the total. Furthermore, this paper explores the potential for incorporating curve fitting and string matching, two other machine learning and data processing techniques, to improve constraint screening. Our findings suggest that, although these methods do not outperform our end-to-end supervised learning approach, they can still be used as efficient stopping criteria to prevent excessive computational expenditure, especially when combined with the learned model. It's worth noting that this paper employs a real-world dataset from a European transmission system and uses a real-time unit commitment solver as the baseline for comparison, thereby ensuring the results are consistent with the requirements of practical unit commitment problems. With the solution of large-scale unit commitment problems becoming increasingly crucial for renewable energy integration and operational planning, our research provides valuable insights into how machine learning can facilitate the efficient use of renewable resources. This work has been accepted for publication in the journal Computers & Operations Research. Our initial findings were presented at the 2021 IEEE PESGM conference, where a comparative study revealed the superiority of supervised learning for constraint screening, and this research provides a comprehensive analysis of the method, including the model architecture, parameter optimization, and curve fitting and string matching extensions. Our source code and pre-trained models are publicly available on the GitHub platform, specifically at the repository address https://github.com/edwinmuller/end-to-end_constraint_screening. Users can replicate our experimental results by running the code, and we invite the community to contribute to the development of this important constraint screening approach for unit commitment problems. This contribution extends the application of supervised learning to constraint screening, and our code provides a starting point for further research in this area, promoting the collaboration of the energy community in finding innovative solutions to unit commitment problems. few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes from support sets often struggle due to outliers. This research proposes an effective solution by introducing a model that dynamically weighs support items according to their similarities to query points. The novel method, called Self-Similarity Net (SSN), calculates a dynamic weight for each support item based on its feature similarity to the target, thus making it more adaptable and efficient than existing methods that rely on fixed or average calculations. The SSN model consists of two main components: a multi-layered graph auto-encoder that helps recognize potential outliers by identifying items with weak feature similarities to the target, and a calculator that dynamically weighs support items based on their similarities to the target. The dynamic weight can then be applied to calculate prototypes from support sets using operations such as means, medians, and means of geometric transformations. The proposed model has been rigorously tested using the miniImagenet, tiered-Imagenet, CIFAR-FS, and tiered-CIFAR datasets under different few-shot learning scenarios, showing its superiority over existing methods. One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among consecutive frames exacerbates the forecasting problem. The main objective here is to develop a motion representation that accurately captures the dynamic changes between frames and between areas, which is particularly crucial for predicting individual object movements. Unlike existing motion estimation methods focusing on static images or sequential frames, this study proposes a motion model that integrates both space and time, incorporating detailed pixel-level appearance and high-level object-level correlation to predict future motions systematically. The proposed model is built on a motion causality graph where each node represents an object of interest and their interactions, and each edge signifies the causal influence one object may have on another. The model utilizes a soft constraint that ensures the total causative effect on a given object equals one, signifying exclusive influence. The method allows for incorporating prior knowledge, and for situations where prior knowledge is limited or inaccurate, this study also presents an alternative motion representation approach. The method is simple to implement and can be trained end-to-end using standard optimization techniques. The study evaluates the proposed method using real-world videos and provides a detailed comparison of its performance against other existing motion estimation methods. The results show that even without incorporating detailed meteorological data, this study's temporal motion representation method significantly surpasses current standards in accuracy. The method is versatile and can be applied to predicting not only object positions, but also their expected states and behaviors. The study also presents an application extension of the method, where it differentiates between real and fabricated video content. The method's performance results indicate a notable 75.4% accuracy improvement over current existing methods. While in most FeSCs superconductivity is triggered by a structural nematic transition, PuFe2As2 is a notable exception. Instead, it exhibits a magnetic and nematic phase transition similar to its sister compound LiFeAs, yet its unconventional superconducting ground state is distinct from the asymptotic nodal superconductivity found in LiFeAs. A recent study, using inelastic neutron scattering, reveals that asymptotic magnetic fluctuations are absent in PuFe2As2 above its magnetic transition temperature. The absence of external intervention in reinforcement learning enables agents to engage in autonomous exploration and learning. External guidance in the form of a teacher or expert can enhance efficiency by facilitating better decision making. Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. However, the traditional Hoare logic framework necessitates the
compositional redefinition of many commonly used software functions in order
to ensure they meet specified runtime constraints, a time-consuming and
perplexing process. This research proposes an innovative solution by integrating
software libraries into formal verification via abstraction-based reasoning
techniques. Our method utilizes runtime checks and abstract interpreters to
ensure that library functions, whose internal details remain unverified, do
not violate runtime constraints defined within high-level specifications.
Notably, the proposed method does not necessitate the explicit definition of
all library functions. Additionally, the theoretical concepts underlying this
research have been successfully applied to a practical case study on a real-world
Android app, as demonstrated through testing on actual Android apps. The results
of this study, including the associated code, have been made publicly available.

The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. Various formal and informal frameworks aim to address this need, each defining specifications in unique ways. One key challenge lies in incorporating these diverse specifications into a single system, making it possible to verify the satisfaction of multiple expectations. This paper explores a novel solution to overcome this challenge by designing a unified specification framework, allowing users to automatically verify multiple specifications within a single implementation. Our approach, known as CSML, enables the unified specification of diverse metrics, including real-valued functions, sets, and boolean statements. CSML ensures that any computer-usable definition is convertible into a predicate applicable to computer executables. An automated verifier is incorporated to enforce the satisfaction of these unified specifications. Ultimately, the goal is to empower computer users to rely on reliable, specification-based technologies, free from the complexities and additional costs associated with multiple, disparate verification tools. For more information on CSML, refer to to https://github.com/SpecMLorg/CSML. This link leads to a shared repository containing the formal, machine-readable specification, along with the underlying proof evidence, as well as the verification tool used to enforce the correctness of CSML. Although CSML is primarily centered on executable specifications, it does not limit users from defining non-executable, theoretical specifications that cannot be processed by computers. However, CSML does not currently support the unified specification of hybrid expectations combining both theoretical and executable aspects. This limitation is intended to be addressed in a future iteration. As part of CSML's development, a new programming paradigm is introduced, centered on the verification of unified specifications. This innovative approach is built upon higher-order logic and integrates the principles of lambda calculi, allowing for the conversion of non-executable specifications into executable-dependent specifications. An automated tool, based on higher-order inductive synthesis, is incorporated to prove the underlying evidence for CSML's success. To achieve this, the underlying proof is expressed in a formal, machine-readable language. Notably, the underlying proof evidence for CSML's correctness is itself a unified specification. in approximating Q-functions that don't meet this condition. Despite EMA being straightforward and having

which consumers self-regulate their behavior to minimize energy costs based on real-time prices and weather forecasts. In this context, the energy supplier adjusts the distributed thermal demand in response to varying prices in pursuit of maximum profit. The study presents a predictive model of consumer behavior that seeks to explain this strategy and its impact on supplier profits and energy system efficiency. Using numerical analysis, the model's accuracy is evaluated, and its implications for suppliers and consumers are considered. The results indicate that consumers who self-regulate their behavior in response to prices reduce their energy consumption during periods of high prices and bad weather, yielding lower overall demand. Consequently, the energy supply becomes more stable, and suppliers can generate greater profits if they can predict consumers' behavior. However, this self-regulation leads to increased losses due to the heat transfer process. If suppliers could precisely forecast consumption, they could mitigate these losses by adjusting their supply strategy, but this advantage is diminished when considering the thermal system's overall efficiency. In this case, the best outcome occurs when consumers submit unconditional demand and suppliers adjust their supply strategy. This result holds under both price and weather uncertainties. The study's conclusions serve as a reference for suppliers and consumers seeking to maximize their gains in the context of smart grids. We found that in these models, the correlation between bulk and boundary properties persists even with arbitrary levels of disorder, but the extent of this persistence decreases asymptotically as the level of disorder increases.
We established a formula to measure the bulk-boundary overlap by calculating the average squared eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian's eigenfunctions at the disorder average and the boundary, and showed that this formula can be applied efficiently to determine the bulk-boundary overlap in more complex models.
We tested this formula through case studies of disordered two-dimensional topological insulators of orders three and four.
We discovered that while disorder may cause some eigenfunctions' support sets to expand, these eigenfunctions remain partially localized at the boundary.
We found that the characteristics of these partially localized eigenfunctions, such as their Fourier transforms and entanglement entropies, are similar to those of generic eigenfunctions, including those associated with zero modes.
We concluded that the bulk-boundary overlap can be accurately estimated from bulk samples with relatively small amounts of disorder, and that the required amount of disorder is much lower than in the case of weak topological insulators. 
Specifically, the required amount of disorder is directly proportional to the square of the disorder class for both second- and third-order topological insulators, but is linearly proportional to the disorder class for fourth-order topological insulators. 
For comparison, the required amount of disorder in the case of weak topological insulators is quadratically proportional to the disorder class. 
Finally, the required amount of disorder in the case of third- and first-order topological insulators is linearly proportional to the disorder class.

A challenging data set has been devised to test the ability to detect actions based on their temporal properties, such as duration and position in time. This challenge employs a unique representation of actions where the type of action is mapped to a unique ID, ignoring spatial variations, while temporal variations are preserved as intensity data. Such a representation can potentially be used in new applications, such as retrieving videos of actions over long periods, such as athletic events analysis. Our initial approach to this challenge relies on using state-of-the-art network that can perform tasks such as semantic segmentation and object proposal generation, and we have found that standard networks can be converted with minimal adjustments to accommodate the new representation. Using our conversion, we have achieved good results on standard test sets and have also demonstrated the potential of our representation to facilitate tasks such as temporal action localization and duration estimation. As an added benefit, we have found that our conversion can improve the quality of standard bounding box based results, such as by increasing the precision of action type classification. Since our test set is focused on temporal properties, we have found that standard bounding box based results are lacking and we have therefore developed a new evaluation metric to facilitate fair comparison of different approaches to this challenge. This metric attaches importance to video action detection accuracy in cases where the duration of the action on both training and testing data varies widely. This is in contrast to the standard IoU metric which we have found to be biased towards models which only perform well on testing data with similar properties to that found in conventional data sets. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, completing clustering on 50,000 data points in around 320 nanoseconds with 2,000 qubits. "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to be taken. These actions may relate to who the mafia members are targeting for night killings or who the living citizens are choosing for investigations during the day. The game continues until one group is eliminated, with the mafia seeking to overpower the citizens or vice versa. We introduce "Bee the Defender," an original "Mafia" variation. In "Bee the Defender," the mafia and citizens participate in the classic "Mafia" dynamics with the addition of "Bee" actions that can be taken by either team. "Bee" actions enable a designated player to safeguard another from the consequences of the night phase. Our research focuses on analyzing "Bee the Defender," with a 3-bee variant for 9-player games. We develop a strategy for the 3-bee variant that ensures the mafia will always prevail, breaking the fundamental symmetry of the "Mafia" dynamic. It has been discovered that FUV and NUV emissions from NGC 4147 originate not only from stellar sources but also from the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM). These integrated magnitudes, however, differ significantly from those obtained from the FUV and NUV photometry across the entire UV spectrum. This discrepancy highlights the fact that while photometric methods allow us to determine the fraction of UV-emitting stars with smaller statistical errors, photometry fails to correct for stellar atmospheric transparencies and interstellar medium (ISM) effects. The majority of the remainder comes from AGB and post-AGB stars as well as other unknown sources. The prevalence of these non-HB sources renders constraints based on integrated UV luminosity relations of little value for estimating HB star numbers. These limitations could, however, be addressed by conducting deeper UV photometric studies that allow for the accurate identification of contributing sources. This would not only correct for ISM effects but would also account for non-HB sources and other stars such as white dwarfs and subdwarfs that may be contributing to the total UV emission. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD require a revised approach. Although conceivably, diverse services can be converted to WSDL/SOAP formats, this method is impractical and ignores the significant costs involved. An alternative is needed to effectively orchestrate these modern services. This research proposes the introduction of a service gateway, implementing the gateway pattern to provide a solution to this problem. Two real-world examples are presented to demonstrate how a service gateway can achieve this goal, one utilizing RESTful principles and the other applying microservice standards. By examining these cases, we can gain a deeper understanding of both the benefits and limitations of service gateways, as well as how they accommodate different patterns. Furthermore, we explore how a service gateway can be viewed as a specific type of process. This work also explores the related design patterns that utilize a service gateway, as well as the potential for a standardized interface like OASIO to facilitate integration. Ultimately, while a service gateway can alleviate some costs, it also introduces new expenses and complexities. As a result, we suggest that a more universal, cross-motivation orchestration approach remains an area for future investigation. These devices allow users to shoot scenes while moving, making it common for objects in the scene to enter the frame from the user's perspective. While capturing scenes from user-centric view, the line at the horizon may not remain horizontal due to the user's movement and posture. However, existing panoramic alignment methods fail to consider the horizon line's non-uniform appearance in images, leading to imperfect results when assessing alignment using test images featuring prominent horizons. This paper introduces a novel metric called the Panoramic Alignment Score (PAS), which can effectively assess panoramic alignment by taking into account diverse types of images. This method also considers horizons with non-uniform textures and can be applied to both synthetic and real-world test images featuring various prominent and non-prominent panoramic scenarios. Our research demonstrates that the PAS has improved performance compared to the current state-of-the-art metrics for evaluating panoramic alignment. Additionally, we found that the majority of test images, including those with non-prominent horizons, feature a uniform or close-to-uniform panoramic alignment. Conversely, the test images with a non-uniform and prominent panoramic alignment are often characterized by weak lights, long stretches of texture, or a combination of strong and weak textures. These prominent cases may occur naturally in scenarios such as a yellow line on a race track or a weak grid pattern. Our research also highlights the benefits of utilizing datasets that have not been pre-processed to avoid over-fitting and can improve the model's performance. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector was implemented with a modified structure, incorporating six slim endcap sensors to extend its scope to the forward area. As part of the CMS revival following the 2021 Long Shutdown, the upgraded forward pixel detector was reintroduced, with fine-grained sensors positioned at a 5.0 cm distance from the CF4 gas-filled barrel, closely encircling the beam line. As the innermost component of the CMS detector, the pixel detector plays a pivotal role. As such, this paper outlines the procedures and physics evaluation of the pixel detector's calibration. Initially, the analysis focused on the determination of the pixel detector's position relative to the center of the detector (off-center correction). Following this, the analysis evaluated the consistency of pixel clusters (pixel detector internal quality) using event pile-up. Furthermore, the analysis tracked the integrated charge per hit as well as its magnitude over the course of the integrated charge (gain) along the sensor's sensing layer. As the pixel detector's position relative to the beam line is not monitored by luminosity sensors, the analysis evaluated the beam line proximity predictions based on the position of pairs of hit clusters in relation to their proximity to the beam line. Lastly, the analysis evaluated the quality of sensor regions near the sensing edge (edge regions). As the edge regions exhibit heightened levels of radiation, the results of this analysis serve as an indicator of the potential degradation of the sensing quality in these regions, with the aim of establishing a correlation between the sensing quality and radiation levels, as well as other factors such as sensing edge proximity and dose received. This research was conducted making use of data obtained from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, collected over the course of 2020. As a result, the sensing quality in relation to radiation levels of 16, 32, and 103 nA·cm² over the course of 2020 was measured. When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain instances, saturation momentum can be determined through a straightforward mathematical calculation in scenarios with high-energy hadrons.  In a specific instance involving a high-energy proton-proton collision, the calculation yields a saturation momentum directly proportional to $\sqrt{s}$, the center-of-mass energy.  As another example, the calculation in a high-energy proton-nucleus collision shows that the saturation momentum is directly proportional to $\sqrt{s}\,A^{1/3}$, where $A$ represents the atomic mass number.  However, in a normal proton-proton or proton-nucleus collision, the calculation fails to accurately predict saturation momentum; instead, it only provides an approximation in a logarithmic power series.  In an attempt to bridge this gap and better understand the behavior of saturation momentum, three distinct models are introduced.  These models, based on geometric and energy arguments, help to clarify a notable discrepancy between predicted and observed saturation momenta in proton-proton collisions.  In particular, the discrepancy concerning the energy dependence of saturation momentum in proton-proton collisions can be resolved if saturation momentum follows a geometric scaling pattern.  Within the geometric scaling framework, the calculation reveals that the scaling variable is directly linked to $\sqrt{\t s}/p_T$, where $\sqrt{\t s}$ represents the transverse energy from the collision and $p_T$ is the average transverse momentum.  In contrast, the variable for proton-nucleus collisions is $\sqrt{2\t s/n_T}$, where $n_T$ is the nucleon transverse momentum.  In general terms, the geometric scaling applies to collisions involving nucleus-proton, and the use of distinct scaling variables based on specific $\t s$ and $p_T$ values enables the calculation of saturation momentum in various processes.  In particular, the calculation shows that the scaling variable for nucleus-proton collisions is directly proportional to $x_B \alpha_s^2 N_c A^{1/2}$, where $x_B$ represents the Bjorken-x, $\alpha_s$ is the QCD coupling constant, and $N_c$ represents the number of quark colors.  In contrast, the scaling variable for proton-proton collisions is directly proportional to $x_B \alpha_s^2$ but fails to accurately predict saturation momentum due to limitations in calculating terms

A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. Further, we obtain sufficient information to determine the local existence of deformations for nearly G2-manifolds of compact domain with a real Killing spinor and four-dimensional dimension. Lastly, we derive explicit formulas for the deformation space of abstract G2-manifolds and Riemannian metrics, providing a decisive conclusion about their non-existence. Furthermore, we prove that a deformed G2-manifold can be constructed from its infinitesimal deformation of the metric, but a similar approach for deforming the G2-structure itself yields a negative outcome. To analyze the deformation of instantons, we introduce a new operator that governs the deformation space and utilize it to show that homologically non-degenerate G2-instantons are rigid. To establish the local existence of deformed instantons, a limiting process is employed to translate the homotopy formula for deformed instantons on a domain to its equivalent form on the boundary, a Riemannian metric. We find that the deformation space of instantons is isomorphic to that of the deformed metric on the boundary. Lastly, we utilize the fact that deformed spinors on a domain converge to a deformed spinor on the boundary, a characteristic of the limiting process to derive the deformation of abelian instantons, a result that demonstrates the inability to deform them. To verify the existence of deformed G2-instantons of order k, a recursive formula for the operator that governs the deformation of instantons is introduced, a formula which indicates their potential existence. However, a formula that analyzes the instantons' contributions to the operator that governs the deformation of instantons reveals that, at a minimum, k must equal the instantons' codimension for such deformations to be possible. For such deformations to be trivial, k must equal zero, a condition that is only feasible if the instantons exhibit rigidity, a property which indicates the inability to deform such instantons.

The direct conversion of C code into executable code requires both a reliable translation process and guarantees that the generated code is free from runtime errors. To address this challenge, our solution utilizes ACL2's hybrid proof capabilities, translating C code into a form that combines both operational and relational semantics, and applies partial evaluation to ensure the free variable values used in the translation match the actual values executed at runtime. The underlying proof strategy utilizes function summaries to establish trust in the generated C code. The implementation of our solution is built upon ACL2's pypeeclsp translator, and as a result, the accompanying C code and theorems are compiled into executable EECLC files. The correctness of our tool has been empirically validated through successful verifications of five non-trivial programs, two of which compute the Fibonacci sequence, one searches for prime numbers, and two evaluate mathematical functions. By leveraging the hybrid nature of relational proofs in ACL2, our approach involves defining functional and relational declarations for each procedure, and then utilizing partial evaluation to ensure correct operational behavior. The anonymity of comments on platform-wide feeds can make them developers' primary source of information on software projects, although this is not widely acknowledged. Our investigation delves into the inner workings of comments on platform-wide feeds, referred to as "wall-of-shame," which are viewed as humorous by developers, with a focus on their underlying structure. We employ a grounded theory approach to analyze an open-source comment history of 1 million across five developer platforms, revealing that comments are driven by software project issues that developers perceive as laughable. Our findings also suggest that developers strategically use comments as a form of public criticism, which is otherwise reserved for private online comments. The implications of our study are that software projects considered "mature" may hide the true extent of issues discovered by developers, which are subsequently commented on anonymously. On the other hand, developers' preference for humor over criticism within the community may have a negative impact on the overall well-being of the community. Our study provides a framework for understanding the underlying structure of comments on platform-wide feeds and offers a framework for managing project issues in a way that balances humor with constructive feedback. Ultimately, this can help create a more positive software development community. Our study provides an initial step in investigating an under-researched area of software development, which we believe warrants further exploration, particularly in investigating potential connections between developers' humor and community satisfaction. In a study published in The Astronomical Journal, researchers reported multiple low-frequency radio emissions from M dwarf stars, a phenomenon observed across the frequency range spanning from 60 to 180 MHz. In a new investigation, we examine frequency interlocks in these systems and discuss their potential association with periodic radio emissions, the rotation periods of stars, and other astrophysical effects. Our analysis reveals two possible explanations for these interlocks: (1) their occurrence is coincidental, driven by random fluctuations and the limited number of data points, or (2) low-frequency radio emissions from M dwarfs may be a manifestation of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence driven by stellar rotation. While the first explanation appears more plausible, especially at higher frequencies, the second hypothesis could possibly account for the observed frequency interlocks and is potentially linked to periodic radio emissions seen at higher frequencies. If confirmed, this would indicate that low-frequency radio emissions from M dwarfs may be a manifestation of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence driven by stellar rotation. Our analysis also highlights the requirement for larger data sets, comprising hundreds of frequency interlocks, to conclusively determine the origin of these interlocks. Lastly, we discuss the possibility that future low-frequency radio emission surveys may uncover numerous additional M dwarfs capable of producing low-frequency radio emission. Based on existing data sets, we predict that such surveys will yield an approximate thirty-fold increase in the number of known M dwarfs capable of producing low-frequency radio emission. Our predictions are based on several hypothetical scenarios, including the assumption that low-frequency radio emission is uniformly distributed across all M dwarfs. If confirmed, this would indicate that about seven percent of M dwarfs within our galaxy could potentially produce low-frequency radio emission. Our predictions also highlight the requirement for large follow-up surveys to study and understanding the origin, characteristics, and spectral distribution of low-frequency radio emission from M dwarfs. These surveys should be designed to incorporate high-collimation high-sensitivity instruments, capable of producing frequency resolution comparable to or better than the frequency spacing of the Parkes Multibeam Receiver. Our prediction also suggests that such follow-up surveys will yield substantial data sets, comprising hundreds of frequency spacings, allowing for the unambiguous identification of natural and possibly artificial frequency interlocks and their differentiation from random fluctuations. Yet, a closer examination reveals that when queries are reformulated as completed sentences and fed into the model's next-word prediction function, the results of which can be ranked, often yields better outcomes than traditional retrieval-based methods. This new paradigm, which we call "zero-shot ranking" (ZSR), allows for the direct assessment of the efficacy of language models as knowledge bases. For instance, when posed with the query "Water is made up of...", the model correctly identifies the answer "one hydrogen and one oxygen atom" without any external training or fine-tuning. Interestingly, while GPT-3 excels in this context, smaller models, such as RoBERTa and BART, also prove effective in ZSR-based queries. Importantly, our results suggest that these smaller models can outdo GPT-3 in cases where the model's knowledge retrieval is not merely a matter of verbatim string matching. As such, ZSR presents a fresh avenue for the innovative use of language models as knowledge sources. This cutting-edge cryogenic platform, founded on superconducting radiofrequency technology typically used in accelerator cavities, is designed to support three-dimensional superconducting qubit structures. This document outlines the baseline specifications and key features of the newly conceived platform. Compared to the existing single-spacer prototypes at Fermilab, this design enhances thermal conductivity, reduces thermal loss through improved thermal isolation, and facilitates heat exchange based on the principles of heat radiation over a large surface area. Initially, the experimental space will accommodate a single qubit. However, the flexibility of the design will allow for easy expansion to accommodate multiple spacers, each supporting one or more qubits. Moreover, the large experimental space will offer ample room to accommodate complicated 3D qubit structures and allow for movement and rotation of magnetic resonators, enabling precise magnetic field homogeneity and reducing thermal conductivity. This work marks the beginning of a design that addresses the cryogenic needs of future quantum computing applications. Our team is currently exploring various modifications to further optimize this concept. This document outlines various modifications under consideration. This study examines crypto APIs in 1,025 open-source.NET projects and discovers that even skilled developers fall short in utilizing crypto APIs correctly. Across all projects, 20% exhibit some form of misuse of crypto APIs, including 4% that introduce security vulnerabilities. A range of issues was found, including incorrect usage of hash and encryption functions, failure to update Hashing and Encryption objects, and improper handling of Key objects. The study highlights the need for continued education and awareness-raising regarding secure use of crypto APIs, even in established software projects. It also serves as a reminder that best security practices are not always adopted, even by experienced developers. Analyzing high-impact storm events, the evidence suggests that wave height is more strongly correlated with satellite wind speed than with the standard wave measurement system, with these associations remaining significant across various storm durations. This finding is particularly relevant when considering the accuracy of satellite wind speed readings over ocean areas where wave measurement devices are lacking, creating a significant data gap for wave height estimates during extreme weather events. With access to unlimited financial resources, the study estimates that wave height estimates could be further improved by up to 15% by combining satellite and buoy wind speed data, while conventional estimates are flawed and inaccurate, resulting in significant errors of up to several meters for high-impact storms. In the zonal problem, $\dot{A}_Z(\tau)$ varies between 0.27 and 1.53 deg/min, with higher values related to more eccentric orbits and lower values associated with more circular orbits. For a given orbit, $\dot{A}_Z(\tau)$ reaches its maximum when the semi-major axis is at its minimum, specifically when it equals 0.27 deg/min. By combining these observations with theoretical models, we infer that the majority of the radiation responsible for the 1300 \AA suppression originates $\sim$2.84 $\pm$ 0.16 AU from the star. Although our findings do not indicate AU Mic b's atmosphere is being heavily impacted, this may change if the planet's orbit shrinks due to gravitational interactions with companion AU Mic c. Our discovery marks the first detailed UV observation and analysis of a planet's atmosphere under its parent star's intense X-ray and UV radiation. Future studies should observe this system during X-ray outbursts to better understand these impacts. Additionally, our proposed photometric analysis of AU Mic's UV spectrum reveals no evidence of the planet producing an optical H I Lyman-alpha emission spectrum. Moreover, our results imply that AU Mic b and c may not be hot Jupiters; instead, they could be closer to the boundary between Jupiters and Neptunes. Finally, our study highlights the significance of monitoring AU Mic and other young stars during X-ray outbursts to better understand these impacts. This tailored scheme for molecules efficiently evaluates electronic integrals using a modified scheme, similar to PBC (Periodic Boundary Conditions) applied to atoms. The implementation details of this method are described in the context of LIBCASSCF, a library providing efficient calculations of electronic structure properties. The method provides a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Results indicate that this approach yields nearly identical outcomes to a refined grid-based method while requiring significantly less computational effort. The method's accuracy was validated against a rigorous reference calculation in a system involving (CO)_4 and was further applied to various complex molecules, including malonaldehyde, the hydroxyl radical, the hydrogen bond dimer of formic acid, and a stacked pair of the planar tetrakisphosphinomethyne molecule. The calculated energy corrections for basis set superposition and dispersion accounted for a substantial fraction of the interaction energy in these systems. The method provides a computationally efficient tool for quantifying basis set superposition error and dispersion interactions in complex molecules. The implementation of this method in LIBCASSCF now enables the efficient computation of these interactions in coupled-cluster calculations. The LIBCASSCF implementation of this method is complemented by a graphical interface that visualizes the partitioning of the C(2x2) density matrix between two molecules. This interface helps to understand the origin of the basis set superposition error and dispersion in molecular interactions. For instance, in malonaldehyde and the hydroxyl radical, the local density matrix analysis revealed that the basis set superposition error and dispersion accounted for a significant fraction of interaction energy. However, in the formic acid dimer, the hydrogen bond dimer of formic acid, and the tetrakisphosphinomethyne dimer, the interaction energy was predominantly driven by dispersion. The method now enables the efficient calculation of these interactions in complex systems. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard in 1978. Several approximation algorithms have been developed to solve this problem, but only a few are known to provide a guaranteed, non-decreasing solution. The currently best-known algorithm provides a guaranteed solution with a value of at most k plus the minimum possible integer value between k and n minus k plus one. The current best-known algorithm for solving the Metric Dimension problem has a runtime complexity of O(n^2.59). We present a randomized, polynomial-time algorithm that can solve this problem, and also provide a unique, known polynomial-time algorithm for tree graphs. The runtime complexity of our algorithm is O(n^2 * (k-n + 1) + nk^2). The algorithm we use is similar to previously known algorithms for solving this problem, based on dominating sets, but with some modifications to the algorithm's steps and a unique way of selecting the dominating set itself, aimed at reducing the size of the set as much as possible. The algorithm we use has a runtime complexity of O(nk^2 + n^2*(k-n + 1)). First, we add vertex i to the dominating set itself if, for any two vertices j and v, a unique vertex i is positioned at different distances from the two vertices j and v. If no such vertex exists, we remove vertex i from the dominating set itself if, for any vertex j and vertex v, a unique vertex i is positioned at different distances from the two vertices j and v, and also if there is no vertex in the dominating set itself which is positioned at different distances from the two vertices j and v. If such a unique vertex i exists, we remove it from the dominating set itself. If no such unique vertex exists, we remove the last added vertex from the dominating set itself. If such a unique vertex i exists and also if vertex i is positioned at different distances from the two vertices j and v, we remove vertex i from the dominating set itself, and also update the set itself to only include vertex i. If no such unique vertex exists, we remove the last added vertex from the dominating set itself. If the desired size of the set itself has not been reached, we return to the initial steps of the algorithm itself

growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning and causing unnecessary delays and costs. To overcome these issues, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process data for underground infrastructure systems. Its approach involves dividing the city into a grid and assigning a node and arc representation, with each node holding critical attributes such as cost and availability. This allows for the computation of key performance indicators and reveals that a general solution can never be optimal if there are multiple infrastructure systems. A scalable distributed solution is proposed to address this challenge. A test case from Toronto, Canada, demonstrates that GUIDES can facilitate rapid underground infrastructure system planning and efficient decision-making among all city stakeholders. Its proposed algorithms have a theoretically efficient, linear-time complexity. Through a computational study, we examine how the scale of the input data affects GUIDES' computation time, revealing a linear relationship. This suggests that GUIDES can easily accommodate a variety of cities based on their land area, population, and number of underground infrastructure systems. To further validate its practical application, we present a real-world case study of a construction project in Toronto, highlighting GUIDES' ability to meet a city's specific planning needs for simultaneous infrastructure system access. This can help a city make informed, data-driven decisions, meet its goal of becoming smart, and better serve its citizens. Ultimately, GUIDES' framework can be adapted and tailored to accommodate the unique requirements of different cities. This is an unpublished paper submitted to the Journal of Urban Technology. A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. Our results demonstrate that the unfolded probabilities are in much better agreement with theoretical predictions than raw ones. For this purpose, it's often necessary to define a structural knowledge framework, determining how different variables and system stages are interconnected. This dual challenge of structure learning and function modeling within complex systems is gaining more attention. While there's been significant progress in developing methods for identifying system functions (i.e., how variables change over time) using data, there's been less focus on this issue compared to the extensive research on structure learning alone. This tutorial-style research demonstrates that addressing this challenge requires both innovative statistical and machine learning techniques, in addition to a diverse array of data from multiple disciplines. This two-part paper explores the latest findings in structure learning methods for complex system functions, covering both theoretical and algorithmic aspects. Part one delves into the theoretical aspects, discussing the challenges of analyzing complex data that often feature issues like missing values, multimodal distributions, and outliers. Part two focuses on the algorithmic aspects, discussing the use of data-driven methods like neural networks, feature extraction, and representation learning to inform structure learning. This research also includes a range of experimental results, showcasing the effectiveness of these methods on various complex system function data sets. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to the growing body of literature on this topic, providing readers with a deeper understanding of the latest findings and a range of methods for learning complex system functions. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture has achieved notable success in various natural language processing tasks. Although it employs a two-stage processing approach, incorporating a retriever and a re-ranker, we have successfully implemented an end-to-end learning scheme for this model. To achieve this, research has established guidelines for selecting suitable workers and gathering quality annotations, which must be conducted in an unbiased manner. To resolve this issue, we have developed an innovative approach where annotations are performed in pairs by two individuals - one provides the annotation and the other evaluates its accuracy. Due to the occurrence of reciprocal biases, where both the annotator and evaluator strive to produce and judge annotations in an unbiased manner, we have established techniques to detect and remove mutually reinforcing groups of workers. Through extensive testing, which involved collecting annotations on over 2,500 videos and over 35,000 words, we have shown that our approach effectively eliminates biases and retains high annotation quality. To verify the absence of biases, we have performed statistical analysis on the annotations, which were found to be consistent with expectations. Additionally, we have compared our approach with the well-established Kague-Li-Mitchell method and discovered that our method not only eliminates biases but also achieves better performance in terms of annotation quality and pool size. Finally, we have outlined the key factors that contribute to the successful application of our approach, including: selecting suitable annotation tasks, maintaining anonymity for workers, providing clear guidelines and instructions, allowing sufficient time for annotations, and ensuring that instructions are easy to comprehend for non-native English speakers. These insights make our approach an attractive alternative for researchers who require reliable and unbiased crowdsourcing annotations. To facilitate future use of our approach, we have documented a comprehensive Python-based implementation, which includes pre-existing code accessible through mechanical turk interface. Notably, the video branch dominates the network at the initial stages to extract comprehensive video semantics, whereas the text branch dominates the network at the later stages to incorporate precise text guidance, with our proposed UA demonstrating superior performance on various text-video retrieval benchmarks, such as MSVD, MSRVTT, and ActivityNet, when compared to cutting-edge text-video retrieval approaches and architectures. Furthermore, extensive ablation research has been conducted to evaluate the impact of proposed UA modules, as well as other design considerations. For instance, we observed that incorporating two distinct attention modules, one focusing on video semantics and the other on text guidance, significantly improves performance, outperforming a single unified attention module. Moreover, we found that simply incorporating an additional global average pooling layer to generate video semantics or text features is less effective in comparison to designing tailored convolutional operators for capturing video semantics and text features. With our proposed UA, we have achieved state-of-the-art results on MSVD, MSRVTT, and ActivityNet, with even better performance than state-of-the-art non-linear text-video retrieval approaches, while our approach features relatively simple architecture design. For instance, we have achieved 71.41% ranking loss and 78.06% CIDEr on MSVD at a much lower computational cost than the current state-of-the-art two-way multi-head attention text-video retrieval approach. For MSRVTT and ActivityNet, we have achieved 40.34% and 51.41% ranking loss and 62.80% and 48.16% CIDEr, respectively, while our approach is entirely end-to-end. The source code for our proposed UA approach can be accessed at https://github.com/mingchen207/Utilization-Attention. As further validation of our proposed UA approach, we have achieved 69.69% ranking loss and 76.69% CIDEr on MSVD at a higher computational cost than the baseline convolutional text-video retrieval model.
